implementation_notes: MockK was built for Kotlin's semantics: mockk<T>() creates a strictly-by-default double so an unprogrammed call fails instead of returning null, every { mock.call(args) } returns/throws programmes it, verify { ... } records the check and confirmVerified(mock) catches stubs that were never used. It handles what the Java frameworks historically could not - final classes by default, object/companion members, extension functions, named arguments and coroutines through coEvery/coVerify - so a hand-written double is unnecessary except for inline functions, which cannot be intercepted at all.
code_sketch:
val warehouse = mockk<Warehouse>()
every { warehouse.hasInventory("Talisker", 50) } returns true

val order = Order("Talisker", 50)
assertTrue(order.fill(warehouse))

verify(exactly = 1) { warehouse.remove("Talisker", 50) }
confirmVerified(warehouse)
pitfalls: Default strictness is the point, but relaxUnitFun and relaxed mocks reintroduce silent defaults; use them per mock and deliberately.
Inline functions cannot be mocked, and on JDK 21+ MockK loads a Java agent dynamically, which prints a warning and can conflict with restrictive dynamic-agent policies.
Spies and mockkStatic may fail on JDK 16+ with InaccessibleObjectException unless the module is opened; mocking interfaces avoids the reflection surface entirely.
